'''John F. Clark''' (born December 12, 1920)<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last1=Astronautics |first1=United States Congress House Science and |title=The Apollo 13 Accident, Hearings...91-2. June 16, 1970 |date=1970 |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office |page=113 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Apollo_13_Accident_Hearings_91_2_Jun/o0oVAAAAIAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=John+F.+Clark+nasa&pg=PA113&printsec=frontcover |access-date=22 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref> was an American [[electrical engineer]], [[physicist]] and [[Atmospheric science|atmospheric scientist]] who served as the second director of [[NASA]]'s [[Goddard Space Flight Center]] from 1966 to 1976. He oversaw NASA's astronomy and planetary science programs as chairman of the steering committee from 1962 to 1965.

Clark was a member of the [[Apollo 13]] Review Board, convened in 1970 to investigate the [[oxygen tank]] explosion that nearly cost the lives of the mission's three-man crew.<ref>{{cite web |title=Historic Personnel: Center Directors - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/history/historic-personnel/ |publisher=NASA |access-date=22 April 2026}}</ref> He was awarded the [[NASA Distinguished Service Medal]], NASA's highest award, in 1969.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Astronautics |first1=United States Congress House Committee on Science and |title=Hearings, Reports and Prints of the House Committee on Science and Astronautics |date=1970 |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office |page=114 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Hearings_Reports_and_Prints_of_the_House/8-U1AAAAIAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=John+F.+Clark+nasa&pg=RA1-PA113&printsec=frontcover |access-date=22 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref> 

== Early life ==
Clark was born in [[Reading, Pennsylvania]] in 1920. He earned a Bachelor of Science in [[electrical engineering]] with honors from [[Lehigh University]] in 1942 and a Master of Science in [[mathematics]] from [[George Washington University]] in 1946.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Center |first1=Goddard Space Flight |title=Goddard: A Year in Review at Goddard Space Flight Center, National Aeronautics and Space Administration |date=1965 |publisher=The Center |page=34 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Goddard/RuI4dzVPvzUC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=John+F.+Clark+maryland+physics&pg=PA34&printsec=frontcover |access-date=22 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref> He received a doctorate in [[physics]] from the [[University of Maryland, College Park]] in 1956.<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr. John F. Clark |url=https://www.nasa.gov/people/dr-john-f-clark/ |publisher=NASA |access-date=22 April 2026}}</ref>

== Career ==
After graduating from Lehigh, Clark joined the [[United States Naval Research Laboratory]] (NRL) as an [[Electronics engineering|electronics engineer]]. He briefly took on an assistant professorship in electrical engineering at Lehigh in 1947 but returned to the NRL in 1948 to study [[atmospheric electricity]]. He became head of the program responsible for using [[Sounding rocket|sounding rockets]] to study phenomena in the atmosphere. Clark was considered an authority on [[atmospheric physics]], particularly regarding the [[ionosphere]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Subcommittee |first1=United States Congress Senate Committee on Aeronautical and Space Sciences NASA Authorization |title=NASA Authorization for Fiscal Year 1960: Hearings Before the NASA Authorization Subcommittee of the Committee on Aeronautical and Space Sciences, United States Senate, Eighty-sixth Congress, First Session, on S. 1582 [and H.R. 7007], a Bill to Authorize Appropriations to the National Aeronautics and Space Administration for Salaries and Expenses, Research and Development, Construction and Equipment, and for Other Purposes |date=1959 |publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office |page=140 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/NASA_Authorization_for_Fiscal_Year_1960/y0RMAQAAIAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=John+F.+Clark+nasa&pg=PA140&printsec=frontcover |access-date=22 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

In 1958, he moved to NASA's Office of Space Sciences and Applications (OSSA) and was appointed director of the geophysics and astronomy programs three years later.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Administration |first1=Estados Unidos National Aeronautics and Space |title=NASA University Program Review Conference |date=1965 |publisher=NASA |page=225 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/NASA_University_Program_Review_Conferenc/Owc_AQAAMAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=John+F.+Clark+nasa&dq=John+F.+Clark+nasa&printsec=frontcover |access-date=22 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Clark |first1=John F. |last2=Haggerty |first2=James J. |last3=Woodburn |first3=John H. |title=Spacecraft |journal=Science Advisory Board |date=1 January 1961 |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20150018537/downloads/20150018537.pdf |access-date=22 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref> He was appointed the director of science at OSSA in 1963<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bergaust |first1=Erik |title=The Next Fifty Years in Space |date=1964 |publisher=Macmillan |page=56 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Next_Fifty_Years_in_Space/SGwhAAAAMAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=John+F.+Clark+nasa&dq=John+F.+Clark+nasa&printsec=frontcover |access-date=22 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref> and was chairman of the Space Science Steering Committee until 1965.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wells |first1=Helen T. |last2=Whiteley |first2=Susan H. |last3=Karegeannes |first3=Carrie E. |title=Origins of NASA Names |date=1976 |publisher=Scientific and Technical Information Office, Nat. Aeronautics and Space Administration |pages=36-37 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Origins_of_NASA_Names/gJM9AQAAMAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=John+F.+Clark+nasa&dq=John+F.+Clark+nasa&printsec=frontcover |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Clark |first1=John F. |title=Space Simulation |journal=Proceedings of the Sixth Space Simulation Symposium |date=1 May 1972 |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19720014600 |access-date=22 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref> He oversaw funding for an [[Mauna Kea Observatories|observatory]] on [[Mauna Kea]], later named after the Dutch astronomer [[Gerard Kuiper]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Letter to Mr. Akiyama from John F. Clark (Director of Sciences, Office of Space Science & Applications) August 26, 1964 |url=https://hilo.hawaii.edu/maunakea/library/ref/2740 |website=hilo.hawaii.edu |publisher=University of Hawaii at Hilo |access-date=22 April 2026}}</ref>[[File:John F. Clark and President Richard Nixon at Goddard Space Flight Center.png|thumb|Clark greeting President [[Richard Nixon]] during his visit to Goddard for a briefing on [[Apollo 13]]]]

Clark became acting director of Goddard Space Flight Center in July 1965 and was appointed its second director on May 5, 1966, succeeding [[Harry J. Goett]].<ref>{{cite book |title=NASA Activities |date=1976 |publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration |page=22 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/NASA_Activities/DyzuLDKwOCwC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=John+F.+Clark+nasa&pg=RA5-PA22&printsec=frontcover |access-date=22 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref> He served for more than a decade, retiring from NASA on July 1, 1976.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Fitzgibbons |first1=Ryan |last2=Nune |first2=Swarupa |title=Goddard at 60 |url=https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/13184/ |access-date=22 April 2026 |agency=NASA Goddard Space Flight Center |date=April 29, 2019}}</ref>

After the explosion of the oxygen tank on Apollo 13, Clark was part of the Apollo 13 Review Board.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Hard-won Triumph of the Apollo 13 Mission - 45 Years Later - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/missions/apollo/the-hard-won-triumph-of-the-apollo-13-mission-45-years-later/ |publisher=NASA |access-date=22 April 2026 |date=3 May 2023}}</ref>

In 1974, Clark accepted the [[Collier Trophy]] on behalf of NASA, jointly with Daniel J. Fink of [[General Electric]], for the [[Landsat program]], for "proving in 1974 the value of U.S. space technology in the management of the Earth's resources and environment for the benefit of all mankind".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Mack |first1=Pamela E. |title=LANDSAT and the Rise of Earth Resources Monitoring |url=https://www.nasa.gov/history/SP-4219/Chapter10.html |website=www.nasa.gov |publisher=NASA |access-date=22 April 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Robie |first1=Bill |title=For the Greatest Achievement: A History of the Aero Club of America and the National Aeronautic Association |date=1993 |publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press |location=Washington, D.C. |page=235}}</ref>

He was a member of the [[American Association of Physics Teachers]], [[American Geophysical Union]], [[Scientific Research Society of America]], and [[Philosophical Society of Washington]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Collins |first1=Martin |last2=Collins |first2=Martin J. |last3=Fries |first3=Sylvia Doughty |title=SPACEFARING NATION |date=17 February 1991 |publisher=Smithsonian |isbn=978-0-87474-907-6 |page=142 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/SPACEFARING_NATION/kYhTAAAAMAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=John+F.+Clark+nasa&dq=John+F.+Clark+nasa&printsec=frontcover |access-date=22 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref> He was awarded the [[NASA Exceptional Service Medal]], [[NASA Outstanding Leadership Medal]], and the NASA Distinguished Service Medal, NASA's highest award.

== Personal life ==
He and his wife had two children. They lived in [[Silver Spring, Maryland]], outside of [[Washington, D.C.]] Clark held four patents in [[Electronic circuit|electronic circuits]].<ref name=":0" />
